The Filipino party game

A card game for the Filipino family party.Chaos included.

Salo Salo Sabotage is a bilingual English and Tagalog card game about throwing the perfect salo-salo while your titas, the typhoon and Filipino Time do their best to ruin it. It's made for family game night, the holidays and every gathering where somebody asks if you've eaten yet.

How it plays

Everyone is hosting. Only one party survives.

Build your salo-salo in front of you: three Food, three Family and three Fun. The first to complete all nine wins. On your turn you draw one card and play one card, so it's easy to pick up in a round or two.

Food3 FoodThe dishes on the table. Kare-kare, lumpia, sisig, halo-halo.
Guest3 FamilyThe people who show up. Ninang, Ate, Tita, Ninong.
Fun3 FunThe mood. Barrel man, parol, pabitin, the mahjong table.

Get all nine and shout “Salo‑Salo!”

The sabotage

Everything that can go wrong at a family party, in card form.

A typhoon wipes out a whole category. The lights go out. Nobody's guests arrive on time. And when Tita shows up with tsismis, somebody's guest walks out.

BagyoName a category and every player loses it, including you.
Filipino TimeNobody's guests can show up for two whole rounds.
BrownoutLights out. No Fun cards for anyone for two rounds.

Who it's for

Made for the table where the whole family sits.

Christmas, Noche Buena and New Year's

Something to do after the food and before the karaoke. It plays in under an hour, so the cousins, the titos and the little ones can all get a round in.

Filipino American families sharing culture at home

The game was made by a Filipino American mom for her son. The Tagalog words are part of the play, so you learn them together by saying them out loud, not by studying them.

A gift for your tita, your barkada or the balikbayan box

A small, beautiful box every Filipino recognizes the minute they open it. A thoughtful Christmas gift, a hostess gift, or a fun add-on for family back home.

Classrooms, Filipino clubs and community events

Teachers, FilAm student groups and cultural organizations use it to start conversations about family, values and language in a way that feels like play.

The culture

The rules come from how Filipino families actually live.

Every counter in the deck is something your family already does. That's why people laugh the first time they read the cards.

Reverse counter

Bahala Ka Sa Buhay Mo

What you say when someone's had enough of you. Someone sabotages you, you send it right back, and they deal with it themselves.

KapwaWelcome the unexpected guest instead of fighting them. Connection turns trouble into blessing.
Utang na LoobCall in a debt of gratitude, and the next two cards drawn come straight to you.
Mano PoThe strongest counter in the deck. Respect stops anything coming your way.
Plastic Sofa CoverGreat for furniture, not so great for whoever sits on it. Blocks the attack, and the saboteur gets stuck.

Questions

Good to know before you order.

Do I need to speak Tagalog to play?

No. The game is in English with Tagalog words woven into the cards, and the full rules include a glossary. Players who don't speak Tagalog pick the words up as they play.

How many people can play, and how long does it take?

Two to five players, ages 8 and up. A game takes about 30 to 45 minutes. New to it? The interactive tutorial walks you through a round with the real cards.

Is it a good gift?

Yes. It comes in a wraparound tuck box with original illustration on every card, and it fits easily in a stocking, a gift bag or a balikbayan box.

Where can I buy it?

Order online and it ships from Cerritos, California with USPS Ground Advantage. Shipping is $5.95 for one game and free on two or more, US addresses only. You can also find it at Seven Syllables Coffee in Cerritos while supplies last.

Can I try it before I buy?

Yes. Play the free browser demo solo against Tita AI, or pass the phone for two players. No download needed.

Who made it?

Salo Salo Sabotage was created and illustrated by Ren Dela Cruz of Salita, a Filipino American author and educator. It's printed in a small run in Richmond, California on FSC-certified recycled paper with soy-based inks.
